kid.question: What kind of water source pictures the Lord?

options.text: A cistern storing rain water
A well dug in stone
A channel carrying river water
A fountain of flowing water

kid.explanation: The Lord calls Himself the fountain of living waters, the source the people have forsaken.

kid.question: What was wrong with the containers the people chose?

options.text: They were cracked and leaked
They were shallow and small
They were distant and hidden
They were deep and narrow

kid.explanation: The people made broken cisterns that could hold no water.

kid.question: What would teach the people how bitter their choice was?

options.text: The lessons of a foreign teacher
The stories of a visiting traveler
The results of their own wrongdoing
The plans of their newest ruler

kid.explanation: The Lord says their own wickedness will correct them and their backsliding will reprove them.

kid.question: What plant does the Lord use to describe Israel's beginning?

options.text: A tall cedar
A good grapevine
A young fig tree
A wild olive tree

kid.explanation: The Lord says He planted Israel as a noble vine with good seed, contrasting its later degeneration.

kid.question: What could not wash away the people's guilt?

options.text: Scrubbing with much soap
Bathing in the distant sea
Waiting for the spring rains
Drinking from a deep well

kid.explanation: Even nitre and much soap would leave their iniquity marked before the Lord.

kid.question: Who is used as a picture of Israel's shame?

options.text: A farmer who loses crops
A soldier who loses armor
A traveler who loses directions
A thief who is caught

kid.explanation: Israel and its leaders are compared to a thief ashamed when found.

kid.question: When would the people call on God to save them?

options.text: When they finished a harvest
When they started a journey
When they were in trouble
When they appointed a ruler

kid.explanation: Though they turned their backs on God, in trouble they would say, 'Arise, and save us.'

kid.question: Whose clothing is mentioned in the comparison about forgetting?

options.text: A priest's linen robes
A king's royal garments
A bride's wedding clothes
A soldier's battle clothes

kid.explanation: The verse asks whether a bride can forget her attire, then contrasts the people's long forgetting of God.

kid.question: What did the people claim about their own behavior?

options.text: They had done no wrong
They had followed bad advice
They had forgotten the rules
They had already made amends

kid.explanation: The people claimed innocence and said they had not sinned; God challenged that denial.

kid.question: What invitation is spoken in Jeremiah 3:1?

options.text: Bring gifts to Shiloh
Come back to Me
Wait outside the temple
Call together the elders

kid.explanation: Despite the charge of unfaithfulness, the Lord says, 'Yet return again to me.'

high-school.question: How do the two water images explain the people's mistake?

options.text: They abandoned a polluted stream for a reservoir awaiting seasonal rain
They abandoned a shared supply for wells owned by neighboring nations
They abandoned a distant spring for storage protected within their city
They abandoned a living source for containers unable to retain water

high-school.explanation: The two evils are forsaking the Lord, the living fountain, and making broken cisterns that cannot hold water.

high-school.question: How does Jeremiah interpret the search for Egyptian and Assyrian waters?

options.text: It demonstrates gratitude for God's guidance through the wilderness
It accompanies forsaking the Lord and brings bitter consequences
It provides the means of repairing damage to Jerusalem's reservoirs
It establishes the people's readiness to return to their own land

high-school.explanation: The questions about Egypt and Assyria sit between the charge of forsaking God and the warning that their own wickedness will correct them.

high-school.question: What relationship does the vine image emphasize?

options.text: A poor beginning has been repaired by careful cultivation
A fruitful plant has been transferred into foreign ownership
A neglected plant has recovered after the coming rains
A sound beginning has been followed by corrupted growth

high-school.explanation: God planted a noble vine of right seed but now confronts a degenerate, strange vine.

high-school.question: Why does the washing image undermine the claim of innocence?

options.text: Outward cleansing cannot erase the wrongdoing God can identify
Outward cleansing proves that the people have already been forgiven
A shortage of cleansing materials prevents the people from worshipping
A shortage of water explains why the people's habits have changed

high-school.explanation: God says guilt remains marked despite much soap, then directs the people to evidence of their conduct in the valley.

high-school.question: What exposes the weakness of the people's chosen objects of worship?

options.text: They appeal to their rulers for rescue after refusing to build more shrines
They appeal to God for rescue after treating wood and stone as parents
They appeal to foreign priests for rescue after abandoning local images
They appeal to neighboring cities for rescue after sharing their offerings

high-school.explanation: The people call wood and stone their parents yet turn to God in trouble. God asks whether their many handmade gods can save them.

high-school.question: What shows that the people's response to correction failed?

options.text: They accepted discipline but postponed rebuilding their homes
They sought instruction but lacked teachers in their cities
They rejected discipline and destroyed their own prophets
They consulted prophets but misunderstood the timing of relief

high-school.explanation: The verse states that they received no correction and that their sword devoured their prophets.

high-school.question: What does the bride's clothing comparison make striking?

options.text: The people remember God through preserving their wedding customs
The people seek God by replacing their costly ornaments
The people honor God by postponing their marriage celebrations
The people forget God despite His place in their lives

high-school.explanation: A bride is not expected to forget her attire, yet God's people have forgotten Him for days without number.

high-school.question: What evidence accompanies the people's claim that they have not sinned?

options.text: The blood of poor innocents is found on their clothing
The property of displaced neighbors is found in their homes
The gifts of foreign rulers are found beside their altars
The records of false judgments are found within their gates

high-school.explanation: The charge concerns innocent blood found in their skirts, followed by their insistence that they have not sinned.

high-school.question: What does the comparison between Egypt and Assyria warn about?

options.text: Changing trade routes will bring prosperity rather than shortage
Changing royal customs will bring unity rather than rivalry
Changing external supports will bring shame rather than security
Changing pilgrimage sites will bring understanding rather than confusion

high-school.explanation: Egypt will shame them as Assyria did, because the Lord has rejected the things in which they place confidence.

high-school.question: What tension appears in the opening of Jeremiah 3?

options.text: An invitation to return accompanies an indictment of unfaithfulness
An invitation to celebrate accompanies proof of renewed faithfulness
A promise of rainfall accompanies praise for the people's shame
A promise of foreign refuge accompanies dismissal of the covenant

high-school.explanation: The Lord exposes persistent unfaithfulness yet invites return; the withheld showers and refusal of shame continue the indictment.

expert.question: Why are the heavens summoned to astonishment?

options.text: The people have discovered a new source beyond their inherited territory
A natural drought has made both the fountain and the reservoirs useless
The people have exchanged a sustaining source for a failed substitute
A foreign invasion has prevented the people from reaching their reservoirs

expert.explanation: The shocking exchange is moral and religious: forsaking the living fountain and constructing cisterns that cannot hold water.

expert.question: How do the rhetorical questions assign responsibility for the nation's plight?

options.text: Their own abandonment of divine guidance lies behind their distress
Their ancestors' route through the wilderness made distress unavoidable
Their inability to identify the neighboring rivers produced their distress
Their failure to preserve foreign alliances alone explains their distress

expert.explanation: The Lord asks whether they procured this by forsaking Him, then describes their wickedness and backsliding as corrective consequences.

expert.question: What do the cultivation and cleansing metaphors jointly deny?

options.text: That present prosperity reflects divine care or can be sustained by work
That present corruption reflects a bad planting or can be washed away
That former captivity can be remembered or followed by renewed worship
That former disobedience can be named or judged before the nations

expert.explanation: The seed was good, so degeneration cannot be blamed on God's planting; much soap cannot erase the guilt now marked before Him.

expert.question: What feature of the animal imagery develops the charge of disloyalty?

options.text: Seasonal migration portrays a commanded departure from the promised land
Helpless confinement portrays innocence under the rule of foreign masters
Restless pursuit portrays persistent attachment to other objects of devotion
Patient labor portrays loyalty despite the loss of agricultural prosperity

expert.explanation: The swift camel and wilderness animal images lead into the people's declaration that they love strangers and will follow them.

expert.question: What irony governs the contrast between the people's posture and petition?

options.text: Those turning toward God ask their handmade gods to leave them
Those calling God their father refuse to seek help in their trouble
Those turning their backs on God ask Him to rise and save them
Those calling wood their father discover that it can rescue them

expert.explanation: The people address wood and stone as parents, turn their backs on God, then ask Him to save them when trouble comes.

expert.question: How does the response about correction answer the people's attempt to plead?

options.text: It points to an innocent generation suffering for unexamined accusations
It grants that inadequate instruction explains the people's religious confusion
It grants that repeated discipline has produced a complete moral change
It points to continued transgression and rejection of prophetic rebuke

expert.explanation: All have transgressed; correction was not received, and their own sword devoured their prophets. Their plea does not overturn that evidence.

expert.question: What does the sequence of wilderness and bridal questions expose?

options.text: A claim of independence joined to prolonged forgetting of God
A misplaced trust in foreign rulers joined to costly display
A deliberate rejection of prophets joined to theft of property
An unexamined reliance on ancestry joined to disregard for neighbors

expert.explanation: God challenges the implied inadequacy of His care, then compares their long forgetting of Him with a bride forgetting her attire.

expert.question: How does the announced judgment answer the preceding claim of innocence?

options.text: The denial shifts the case toward the conduct of past generations
The denial suspends the case until more witnesses can be gathered
The denial limits the case to offenses committed outside the land
The denial itself becomes an added ground for God's case

expert.explanation: After naming innocent blood, God announces that He will plead against them because they say they have not sinned. The denial is itself included in His charge.

expert.question: How does the final warning reinterpret repeated changes of direction?

options.text: They complete a divinely directed journey toward a new place of worship
They shift rejected confidences rather than securing a reliable deliverer
They display the flexibility required to restore an exhausted economy
They bring the people closer to a lasting alliance with both empires

expert.explanation: Egypt and Assyria both become sources of shame; the Lord has rejected the objects of their confidence, so prosperity will not follow them.

expert.question: How does the opening legal analogy interact with the call to return?

options.text: It cancels the invitation by declaring that God no longer addresses them
It heightens the seriousness of betrayal beside the offered return
It establishes that withheld rain is unrelated to the people's conduct
It transfers responsibility for unfaithfulness from the people to the land

expert.explanation: The divorce-and-remarriage comparison underscores defilement, yet the Lord still says to return. The subsequent charges preserve the seriousness of the betrayal.
